whyCorrect: The blank has to state what the researchers' caution implies, and the caution is explicitly about applying the findings to customers generally. The one fact the text gives you about the sample is that every respondent was Serbian and that Serbia has a developing economy — so the limitation is that the survey covers only one point on the economic-development scale. The logical follow-through is that you would need respondents from countries at other levels of development before you could say anything about customers broadly. Choice A says exactly that.

whyWrong.B: This turns a caution into a confident prediction about wealthier countries. The study tested no such country, so it supplies no basis for guessing which way those customers would lean.
whyWrong.C: This is the generalization the researchers warned against, restated as advice to multinational retailers. A sentence introduced by "cautioned against applying the findings to customers generally" cannot end by applying them to customers generally.
whyWrong.D: This misidentifies the limitation as sample size within Serbia. The text flags the sample's national and economic uniformity, not that it was too small, and a larger Serbian group would still be one developing economy.

commonMistakes: Reading only the last clause of the passage and picking whichever choice repeats the study's result, instead of tracking the word "cautioned," which requires the ending to limit the result rather than extend it.
tips: When a completion follows a stated limitation, ask what the study could not observe; the answer almost always names the missing comparison group.

whyCorrect: Two things are being decided at once: the number of the noun after "such," and where the apostrophe goes. The phrase lists two separate measures — median salary and work-life balance — so the plural "metrics" is required. And only one profession is under discussion (statistician), so the singular possessive "profession's" is correct.

whyWrong.B: "Metric" is singular, but the sentence goes on to name two of them, so the count does not match.
whyWrong.C: "Metrics" is right, but "professions'" is the plural possessive, which would mean the salary belonged to several professions; the text ranks one job.
whyWrong.D: This is wrong twice: singular "metric" for two measures, and "professions" with no apostrophe at all, leaving "median salary" with no owner.

tips: Count the items that actually follow the phrase "such ___ as" before choosing singular or plural — the list itself tells you.

whyCorrect: Look at what the sentence already has: a subject, "Land," and no other verb anywhere in it. That means the blank must supply the main verb, and it has to be a finite past-tense form to match "A decade later." "Used" is the only finite form offered; the other three are non-finite and would leave the sentence with no predicate at all.

whyWrong.B: "To have used" is an infinitive, not a conjugated verb, so "Land to have used his technology" is a fragment with no main verb.
whyWrong.C: "To use" is also an infinitive and produces the same fragment.
whyWrong.D: "Using" is a participle; it can modify a subject but cannot serve as the sentence's verb, so "Land using his technology to invent..." never finishes as a sentence.

commonMistakes: Choosing an -ing or to- form because it sounds smooth in isolation, without checking whether the sentence still contains a main verb.
tips: Cover the blank and scan for a conjugated verb; if there is none, the blank must be one.

whyCorrect: The appositive right after the blank — "some Catholic and some Protestant" — is what settles this. Whoever fills the blank has to be a group that could contain both Catholics and Protestants and that ruled England after 1534, which includes queens such as Mary I and Elizabeth I, not just kings. "English rulers that followed" is gender-neutral, is accurate to England in that period, and clearly means the ones who came afterward.

whyWrong.A: "England's following monarchs" reads as "the monarchs listed below" rather than "the monarchs who came after," because following placed before a noun normally points forward in a text, not forward in time.
whyWrong.C: "British" is anachronistic — Britain did not exist as a political unit in the sixteenth century — and "kings" leaves out the queens whose reigns drove the Catholic-Protestant swings the sentence describes.
whyWrong.D: "Kings" again excludes the queens the appositive implicitly covers, and "later-ruling" is a strained compound where a simple relative clause is available.

commonMistakes: Treating all four choices as interchangeable synonyms for "the next rulers" and picking by sound, when the appositive "some Catholic and some Protestant" is quietly ruling out any choice limited to kings.

whyCorrect: Check each side of the blank for a complete sentence. Before it: "In Finland, the Hankasalmi observatory site monitors activity in the upper atmosphere of the northern hemisphere" — subject and verb, complete. After it: "in Antarctica, another observatory site, Zhongshan Station, monitors the sky of the southern hemisphere" — also complete. Two independent clauses need a semicolon, a period, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction, and the semicolon is the only one of those on offer.

whyWrong.A: "And" joining two independent clauses needs a comma in front of it; "hemisphere and in Antarctica" also invites a misreading in which Finland's site somehow monitors Antarctica.
whyWrong.B: With no punctuation the two clauses run together into a fused sentence.
whyWrong.C: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice, and this sentence already uses commas to set off "Zhongshan Station," so a fourth comma buries the real break.

tips: When the second clause opens with a prepositional phrase like "in Antarctica," read past it to find the subject and verb before deciding the clause is a fragment.

whyCorrect: "In 2021, her work was featured at Galerie LeRoyer in Canada" and "the exhibited photographs ... captivated audiences" are both complete sentences, so the boundary between them has to be a semicolon or a period. That narrows it to C and D, and meaning decides between them: the previous sentence claims Svarbová reached audiences beyond Slovakia, and the Canadian exhibition is the example of that claim. "For example" therefore belongs to the first clause, with the semicolon after it.

whyWrong.A: This leaves only commas between two independent clauses — a comma splice.
whyWrong.B: Same splice problem, and it strands "for example" with no punctuation separating it from the following clause.
whyWrong.C: The punctuation is legal, but it attaches "for example" to the wrong clause, making the photographs' effect on audiences the illustration rather than the Canadian exhibition itself.

commonMistakes: Assuming a transitional phrase like "for example" always opens the second clause; it can just as easily close the first one, and the surrounding logic tells you which.

whyCorrect: "That the geographic center of North America lay in the state of North Dakota was conceded by all involved" is a full sentence — the whole "That..." clause is its subject. "Establishing its precise coordinates proved more divisive" is a second full sentence. Two independent clauses with no conjunction between them require a semicolon.

whyWrong.A: A comma between two independent clauses with no coordinating conjunction is a comma splice.
whyWrong.C: A colon signals that what follows explains or specifies what came before, but the second clause contrasts with the first — agreement on the state versus disagreement on the coordinates — so a colon misstates the relationship.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation at all the two clauses fuse into a run-on.

tips: A sentence that opens with "That..." is using that clause as its subject; do not mistake it for a fragment.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank makes a general claim — the statues are "extremely heavy" — and the sentence after it supplies the specific figure that backs the claim up: more than 5 tons each. That is intensification, where the second statement sharpens and confirms the first. "In fact" is the transition that does that job.

whyWrong.A: "In any case" dismisses what came before as no longer relevant, but the weight figure is precisely what supports the previous sentence rather than setting it aside.
whyWrong.B: "Earlier" signals a shift back in time, and nothing in either sentence is being placed on a timeline.
whyWrong.D: "Instead" marks a substitution or correction, which would require the 5-ton figure to contradict "extremely heavy" — it confirms it.

tips: When the second sentence gives a number and the first gives an adjective, the relationship is almost always confirmation, not contrast.

whyCorrect: The sentence after the blank does not add a surprise or a consequence — it explains why the 1920 result was the less accurate one, and it does so with a detail that makes that outcome entirely unsurprising: cardboard and string. "Of course" is the transition for conceding something the reader would expect anyway, which is exactly the tone of "the old measurement used primitive tools."

whyWrong.A: "Ultimately" signals a final outcome at the end of a sequence, but the cardboard-and-string detail is background about the earlier attempt, not the endpoint of anything.
whyWrong.C: "Likewise" claims the two sentences make parallel points, yet the second one contrasts the 1920 equipment with Rogerson's, rather than repeating a similarity.
whyWrong.D: "To that end" introduces an action taken to achieve a stated goal; no goal has been stated, and the 1920 surveyors were not working toward Rogerson's aim.

tips: "Of course" is the right pick when the next sentence supplies a reason the reader would have guessed already.

whyCorrect: Read the two sentences as cause and response. Millions of trips depend on the Metro each year; because of that dependence, officials work to keep all 25 stations in good order. The second sentence is the action that follows from the first sentence's situation, so you need a consequence transition, and "Accordingly" is the only one offered.

whyWrong.A: "For example" would make station maintenance an instance of residents taking trips, but maintenance is something officials do, not a kind of trip.
whyWrong.C: "However" sets up a contrast, and there is none — heavy ridership and careful upkeep point the same direction.
whyWrong.D: "Alternatively" offers a competing option instead of the first one, but maintaining the stations is not an alternative to residents riding the system.

commonMistakes: Picking "However" by reflex whenever two sentences describe different actors; different subjects do not mean opposing ideas.

whyCorrect: The goal is stated in the stem: emphasize a difference between the two sculptures. Scan the notes for the one point on which they are not alike — Open Ended is weathering steel, Strike: To Roberta and Rudy is hot-rolled steel. Only the choice that puts those two materials in contrast does what the stem asks.

whyWrong.A: This emphasizes what the sculptures share — both large, both metal, both Serra's — which is the opposite of the stated goal.
whyWrong.B: This describes only one sculpture, so no comparison of any kind is made.
whyWrong.C: This also covers only one sculpture; naming its material without naming the other's leaves nothing for the reader to contrast it against.

tips: On these note-synthesis items, decide what the stem asks for before reading the choices, then reject any choice that mentions only one of the two things being compared.

whyCorrect: The goal is to compare the causes the two theories propose, so the right choice has to state both causes, not just both theorists. Jacobs's cause is branches breaking off when trees brush together; Ng's is branches halting growth when they detect shade. Choice C puts those two mechanisms side by side in a single contrastive sentence.

whyWrong.A: This contrasts the two theories by name only and calls Jacobs's simply "an alternative theory," never saying what either one identifies as the cause.
whyWrong.B: This states that both men proposed theories about crown shyness, which is true but supplies no comparison of the causes at all.
whyWrong.D: This gives Jacobs's cause in full detail and never mentions Ng's, so there is only one side of the comparison.

commonMistakes: Choosing the longest, most detailed sentence; length is not the criterion, coverage of both sides of the stated comparison is.

whyCorrect: The stem asks for an advantage of the Antelope House site specifically, so you need the note that pairs a feature of that site with a benefit it produced. The notes say Antelope House was built under a rock overhang and that overhanging ledges offered protection from heavy rain and snow. Choice D joins those two notes into a single cause-and-benefit statement.

whyWrong.A: This transplants Mud Springs Pueblo's flat terrain and terraced buildings onto Antelope House, which the notes say was built under a rock overhang — the statement is false.
whyWrong.B: This gives the site's location and dates, which are neutral facts, not advantages.
whyWrong.C: This asserts that the location "provided an advantage" without ever saying what the advantage was, so it announces the goal instead of accomplishing it.

tips: An advantage needs both halves — the feature and what it did for the inhabitants; a choice that names only one is incomplete.

whyCorrect: The colon after the blank means the rest of the sentence defines the word you need. What follows is a clash: a government that kept defaulting on its debts nonetheless ran a bigger surplus than the era's model of fiscal discipline. Those two facts do not fit together, and "incongruity" is the word for a finding whose parts sit oddly with each other.

whyWrong.A: A "harbinger" foreshadows something still to come, but the sentence describes a tension inside the data itself, not a sign of a future event.
whyWrong.B: An "exemplar" is a model case, which would fit only if Philip II's finances neatly illustrated a rule; the point is that they defy the expected rule.
whyWrong.C: "Sanction" means either a penalty or an official approval, and the researchers found a pattern in the numbers, not a punishment or an endorsement.

tips: When a colon follows the blank, define the missing word from the material after the colon rather than from the sentence's general topic.

whyCorrect: Track why most minor planets get only a number: there are over 500,000 of them, so naming each one uniquely is impractical. The sentence already calls that task "already challenging," and the blank has to describe what half a million bodies push it into — something beyond challenging. "Insurmountable" is that escalation.

whyWrong.A: "Substantial" means large or considerable, which is no stronger than "already challenging"; the word "nearly" signals an extreme the task is approaching, and "nearly substantial" is a step down, not up.
whyWrong.C: "Unnecessary" would say naming is pointless, but the sentence explains that naming is too hard, not that nobody wants it done.
whyWrong.D: "Feasible" means achievable, which reverses the logic — if the task were nearly feasible there would be no reason to fall back on identification numbers.

commonMistakes: Ignoring "already challenging," which forces the blank to be a stronger word than "difficult," not a synonym for it.

whyCorrect: The example after the blank does the defining: the mihrab, "which almost all mosques include." A feature found in almost every instance is one that is nearly universal, so the blank is about how widely shared the feature is, not about what it looks like. The following sentence confirms this reading by contrasting shared features with the variety of architectural styles.

whyWrong.B: "Elaborate" describes ornamentation, but "which almost all mosques include" reports frequency, not decorative complexity.
whyWrong.C: "Illusory" means not really there, which contradicts a niche that mosques actually contain.
whyWrong.D: "Idealized" means treated as a perfect model, and the sentence says these features are present, not that they are aspired to.

tips: Let the "such as" example set the meaning; here it reports how many mosques have the feature, so the blank must be a frequency word.

whyCorrect: Unpack the double negative: "the characteristics without which the monarch would have been forced to ___ the throne." These are the traits that legitimize a ruler, so lacking them costs the ruler the crown. The blank therefore needs a verb meaning to give up or lose the throne, and "abandon" is the only choice that does.

whyWrong.A: "Reciprocate" means to return something in kind; a throne is not something given back in exchange.
whyWrong.B: "Annotate" means to add notes to a text, which makes no sense as an action performed on a throne.
whyWrong.D: "Equalize" means to make equal, and there is no second throne or quantity being levelled.

commonMistakes: Reading "without which" as if it were "with which" and looking for a verb about gaining power; the phrasing describes what happens when the legitimizing traits are missing.

whyCorrect: The evidence after the colon is a ranking: "iloveyou" was the eighth most commonly used password in 2019. That measures how many people chose it, so the blank has to describe an approach defined by how widespread it is. "Popular" is the word for that, and it also sets up the contrast with what experts "encourage," which people evidently ignore.

whyWrong.A: "Creative" would suggest inventive password choices, but a password that millions of people pick is the opposite of inventive.
whyWrong.C: "Complex" is what the experts recommend, so the sentence's "Nonetheless" would have nothing to reverse; a complex approach would not favor convenience.
whyWrong.D: "Useful" describes value, not prevalence, and the cited statistic counts users rather than measuring usefulness.

tips: Match the blank to the type of evidence given — a frequency statistic calls for a frequency word.

whyCorrect: Every image in the poem is a request aimed at the sea: "Rock me to sleep," "Just let me drift," and the waves and winds combining into a "soothing slumberous lullaby." The speaker is not describing something that happened but asking for something wanted, and what is wanted is calm. The purpose is to convey that longing for the ocean to produce peace within the speaker.

whyWrong.A: There are no "qualms" anywhere in the poem — the speaker wants to go, not to voice reservations about going, so there is nothing to justify.
whyWrong.B: "Toil and care" is mentioned in a single phrase as what the speaker drifts away from; it is a background detail, not one half of a sustained contrast, and the poem never describes everyday life.
whyWrong.C: "Increasing intensity" requires the desire to build across the poem, but the yearning is at full pitch from "My spirit swoons" onward and does not escalate.

commonMistakes: Picking a choice because it mentions a phrase that appears in the text; "toil and care" is real, but a main-purpose answer must cover the whole poem, not one line.

whyCorrect: Track how the paragraph spends its space. Edwards's play appears in the first sentence only, as a way in; the rest tells you who founded the NEC, how they met, what they set out to build, and what the company has done for Black playwrights since 1967. That is an account of the company's origin and its significance, which is the main purpose.

whyWrong.A: A Raisin in the Sun is mentioned only as the production Ward and Hooks happened to be touring in when they met; the text never claims the play influenced their work.
whyWrong.B: Black Body Blues is the entry point, not the subject — the text says nothing about the play itself beyond calling it atmospheric.
whyWrong.C: The text describes what Ward and Hooks envisioned together but never traces changes in their partnership over time.

tips: When a text opens with a specific example and then leaves it behind, the example is usually the hook and the main purpose lies in what follows.

whyCorrect: The passage moves in three linked steps: the countryside's air and odors, the narrator becoming "forgetful" of papers, offices, his chief and his colleagues, and then his mind filling with "the good things that were sure to come" and "a thousand recollections of childhood." The natural setting is the cause and the release from work plus the turn toward future hopes and past memories is the effect. Choice B states that whole chain.

whyWrong.A: Nothing says he has quit his job or that the countryside is his childhood home; he is on a walk outside Paris and merely remembers childhood.
whyWrong.C: This has him thinking about work for career advantage, but the text says he forgets his documents entirely — the "good things" are unspecified future hopes, not work projects.
whyWrong.D: This frames the experience as a failure — pressing issues left unaddressed and a distraction — while the passage treats the forgetting as pleasurable "enchantment," and it drops the hopeful thoughts about the future.

commonMistakes: Confusing a detail the narrator sets aside (his office work) with the main idea; the passage's subject is the release, not the neglected paperwork.

whyCorrect: Name the two variables in the research question: perceived similarity between the two categories in an extended-brand pair, and likelihood of buying the extension. The team already has the second one — the change in purchase probability they calculated for each of the 30 pairs. What is missing is a measure of the first, so the design must collect similarity ratings for each pair's two categories and correlate them with the probabilities already in hand. That is exactly choice A.

whyWrong.B: This measures brand recognition, not category similarity, and it correlates it with overall purchase frequency rather than with the extension effect the team computed.
whyWrong.C: This also substitutes brand recognition for category similarity, and correlating it with average product cost answers no part of the stated question.
whyWrong.D: This rates a product against other products in the same category, but the question is about similarity between the two categories in a pair, so the ratings would measure the wrong thing.

tips: Study-design items are usually decided by whether the proposed measurement matches the exact variable named in the research question.

whyCorrect: The claim has two parts: the opinion must be Vanya's, and it must have changed. Only choice D contains a before and an after — "I was proud of him and of his learning; I received all his words and writings as inspired" set against "and now? ... A blank! ... I have been deceived." That reversal from admiration to disillusionment is the change the claim describes.

whyWrong.A: This shows a long-standing grievance about never being thanked, and Vanya explicitly says it held "neither in my youth nor now" — evidence of consistency, not change.
whyWrong.B: This is the professor's opinion of Vanya, which reverses the direction the claim requires.
whyWrong.C: This is Vanya's account of his own sacrifices for the estate; it reveals resentment but says nothing about what he used to think of the professor.

commonMistakes: Selecting any quotation in which Vanya criticizes the professor; a change-of-opinion claim needs a quotation that supplies the earlier view as well as the later one.

whyCorrect: The word carrying the whole conclusion is "solely" — the students claim Aasdh expression is the only thing behind cataract differences in wild mice. To weaken that, you need a case where cataract frequency stays put while Aasdh expression varies widely, because then something other than Aasdh has to be doing the work. Choice A supplies exactly that: wild-type mice with a wide range of Aasdh expression but essentially the same cataract frequency as the knockouts.

whyWrong.B: A link between Aasdh and other genes leaves Aasdh at the center of the causal story; it does not show any other factor operating independently of it.
whyWrong.C: Variation in Aasdh expression among wild mice is what the students' conclusion assumes, so this supports the conclusion rather than undermining it.
whyWrong.D: If the two groups differ only in cataract frequency, the deactivated gene is the isolated cause — this strengthens the students' reasoning.

commonMistakes: Attacking the experiment in general instead of the specific overreach; the finding is fine, and only the word "solely" is vulnerable.
tips: When a conclusion says "solely" or "only," the weakening evidence is almost always a case where the named cause varies but the outcome does not.

whyCorrect: The claim is not just that the relationship is strained but that it is "much more strained than it once was," so the quotation must mark a change. The professor's phrase "For the sake of our former friendship" does that in one word: former concedes that the two men were once friends and are no longer, while the request that Vanya leave the room shows the present state.

whyWrong.B: Vanya explicitly says the lack of thanks held "neither in my youth nor now," which reports a grievance that has stayed the same — the opposite of a change.
whyWrong.C: This is a general complaint about the professor's self-pity with no reference to any earlier period, so it establishes friction but not deterioration.
whyWrong.D: The professor's irritation here is aimed at how the household treats him; nothing in it compares the present relationship to a past one.

tips: For "more X than it once was" claims, hunt for a time marker — "former," "used to," "once," "now" — rather than for the strongest display of the emotion.

whyCorrect: Two facts have to be held together. Mammal studies had a higher average effect than fish studies, and every class examined — fish included — contained individual studies whose effects were well above the mammal average. If some fish studies beat the mammal average, they necessarily beat the many mammal studies that sat at or below that average. So some fish studies found larger effects than some mammal studies did.

whyWrong.B: This flips the averages, claiming fish effects are generally more pronounced, when the text says mammal studies averaged larger differences.
whyWrong.C: The text never reports where Shannon's prairie dog study fell relative to any average, so this comparison is not available from the passage.
whyWrong.D: Nothing in the text discusses whether studies characterized the effects as detrimental; the meta-analysis measured whether traits differed, not how they were labeled.

commonMistakes: Treating a difference in averages as a claim about every individual study; an average leaves plenty of room for overlap at the extremes.

whyCorrect: Find the subject of the blank: it is "Fans," not "the film" and not "The Princess and the Frog" — those sit inside the modifying phrase "of the film The Princess and the Frog (2009)." "Fans" is plural, so the verb takes the plural present form "recognize." The adverb "likely" between subject and verb does not change the agreement.

whyWrong.A: "Recognizes" is the singular form, which would need a singular subject; it agrees with the nearby word "film" rather than with the actual subject.
whyWrong.B: "Has recognized" is singular in the present perfect and also puts the recognition in the past, while the surrounding sentences describe an ongoing fact.
whyWrong.D: "Is recognizing" is singular and progressive, describing something in progress right now, which does not fit a general statement about what fans know.

tips: Cross out prepositional phrases before checking subject-verb agreement; the noun closest to the verb is often not the subject.

whyCorrect: Line the two results up against the host counts. Three-host parasites, which need at least two vertebrate species, fell as sea temperatures rose; two-host parasites, which need only one vertebrate, held largely steady. Since vertebrates are the group the text singles out as especially vulnerable to climate change, the reasonable suggestion is that warming-driven shifts in vertebrate populations pushed down the parasites that depend on more of them, while the two-host parasites saw no host change large enough to move their numbers.

whyWrong.A: This has C. kanabus, a two-host parasite, hit harder than Anisakis sp., but the text reports the reverse: two-host abundance was largely stable and three-host abundance declined.
whyWrong.C: The text states that fish and other marine vertebrates are especially vulnerable to climate change, so concluding that the eight fish species were largely unaffected contradicts the premise the researchers are reasoning from.
whyWrong.D: This states the relationship backwards. Parasites depending on more vertebrate species were the ones that declined, so sensitivity to warming rises with the number of vertebrate hosts rather than falling with it.

commonMistakes: Reading "three-host" and "two-host" as the number of vertebrates involved; the text says three-host parasites need at least two vertebrate species and two-host parasites only one, and that vertebrate count is what drives the pattern.

whyCorrect: Notice the comma already sitting after "music clips." That is the closing half of a pair around the interrupting phrase "through a rich combination of text, images, and music clips," so the blank has to supply the opening half — a comma placed after "that," not before it. The relative clause itself is "that ... traces the development of specific musical genres," and it is essential to identifying the resource, so no comma may separate it from "resource."

whyWrong.A: Putting a comma before "that" cuts the essential relative clause off from the noun it defines, and it leaves the interrupting phrase with a closing comma but no opening one.
whyWrong.B: This has the same wrong comma before "that" and simply adds the correct one after it, so the sentence carries one comma too many.
whyWrong.D: The comma after "that" is missing, so the interrupter is closed but never opened, and "that through a rich combination" runs together.

tips: When one comma is already printed in the sentence, ask what it is paired with before deciding where your own comma goes.

whyCorrect: The subject of the blank is "musings," which is plural, so the verb must be the plural present form "fascinate." The long string of words between them — "her book's musings on tenth-century Japanese courtly life" — makes "life" the nearest noun, but "life" is inside a prepositional phrase and cannot be the subject. The present tense is right because the sentence describes an effect the book still has on readers today.

whyWrong.A: "Has fascinated" is singular and so does not agree with "musings."
whyWrong.B: "Fascinates" is the singular present form, agreeing with "life" rather than with the actual subject.
whyWrong.C: "Is fascinating" is also singular, and the progressive form describes something in progress at the moment rather than an enduring effect.

commonMistakes: Letting the noun immediately before the blank set the verb form; here that noun sits inside "on tenth-century Japanese courtly life" and is not available as a subject.

whyCorrect: Look at what comes after the blank: "the radars track ionospheric irregularities and other geospace phenomena" — a complete sentence with its own subject and verb. Everything before the blank is also complete: the observatory sites "number nearly five dozen." A comma cannot join two independent clauses, so the sentence has to break, and "Located across the globe" then works as an introductory participial phrase modifying "the radars."

whyWrong.B: This produces a comma splice — "dozen, located across the globe, the radars track..." leaves two full clauses joined by commas alone.
whyWrong.C: Adding "which are" makes the middle a nonrestrictive clause but still leaves the two independent clauses spliced together by a comma.
whyWrong.D: With no break at all before "the radars track," the two clauses fuse into a run-on.

tips: Before choosing punctuation, test the words after the blank on their own; if they form a sentence, a comma alone is never enough.

whyCorrect: The sentence opens with the participial phrase "Having devised an optical spectroscopy technique...," and whatever noun follows the comma is what that phrase describes. Only a person can have devised a technique, so the subject must be the chemist himself. "Chemist Ahmed Zewail introduced a new scientific discipline known as femtochemistry" places him in that slot and also supplies the antecedent for "he" in the next sentence.

whyWrong.B: The subject becomes "a new scientific discipline," so the opening phrase says the discipline devised the technique — a dangling modifier.
whyWrong.C: The subject is "the introduction," which makes an abstract event the thing that devised the technique.
whyWrong.D: The subject is "Ahmed Zewail's introduction," not Zewail, so the modifier still dangles, and "would be known" wrongly shifts the sentence into a conditional or future-in-the-past frame.

commonMistakes: Accepting a choice just because the person's name appears somewhere in it; the modifier attaches to the grammatical subject, not to any name in the clause.

whyCorrect: "The vessel took six days to dislodge, in part due to its sheer size" is a complete sentence, and "it's as heavy as two thousand blue whales when fully loaded" is another. Because the second clause spells out what "sheer size" amounts to, a colon is the right mark: it signals that what follows explains what came before, and it is also strong enough to separate two independent clauses. The comma after "dislodge" sets off the added reason.

whyWrong.A: This ends with a comma between two independent clauses, which is a comma splice, and it also drops the comma that should set off "in part due to its sheer size."
whyWrong.C: The commas around the reason are fine, but the final comma leaves the two full clauses joined by a comma alone.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation at all before "it's," the two clauses fuse into a run-on.

tips: A colon needs a complete sentence in front of it; check that first, then check that what follows genuinely explains or specifies.

whyCorrect: The first sentence states a goal — avoiding harsh synthetic dyes — and the second describes the action taken to reach it, experimenting with natural dyes. That is a goal-then-response relationship, so you need a transition that carries the goal forward into the action. "With this in mind" does exactly that.

whyWrong.B: "To sum up" announces a summary of points already made, but the second sentence introduces new information rather than recapping the first.
whyWrong.C: "Nevertheless" signals that what follows happens despite the first sentence, yet switching to natural dyes is precisely what her aim called for, not a departure from it.
whyWrong.D: "In actuality" corrects a mistaken impression, and nothing in the first sentence is being corrected.

tips: When sentence one states what someone wanted and sentence two states what they did, look for a purpose or consequence transition, not a contrast.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank is a concession — the painting cannot really show a fourth dimension because human sight is three-dimensional. The sentence after it pushes back, crediting Metzinger with offering "a fascinating glimpse" anyway. You need a transition that acknowledges the limitation and then partly overrides it, and "That said" is the standard move for that.

whyWrong.A: "For example" would make the multiple-perspective technique an instance of the painting's failure to represent four dimensions, but it is offered as the painting's achievement.
whyWrong.C: "In other words" signals a restatement, and the second sentence reverses the first rather than rephrasing it.
whyWrong.D: "Moreover" adds a further point in the same direction, which would mean piling on more evidence that the painting falls short — the opposite of what follows.

commonMistakes: Reading "Of course" in the previous sentence as the writer's real position; "Of course" flags a concession, which almost always sets up a reversal next.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank makes a general claim — the F-5 is "far more aerodynamic" — and the sentence after it gives the number that backs the claim up, a lift-to-drag ratio more than double the Flyer's. Moving from a general statement to the precise figure supporting it calls for "Specifically."

whyWrong.B: "In conclusion" signals the close of an argument, but this is the second of two sentences supplying evidence, not a wrap-up.
whyWrong.C: "However" sets up a contrast, and the ratio figure agrees with the claim it follows rather than complicating it.
whyWrong.D: "Nevertheless" also signals contrast, implying the ratio holds despite the F-5 being more aerodynamic — but the ratio is what makes it more aerodynamic.

tips: A sentence that supplies the measurement behind a preceding adjective almost always takes "Specifically" or "In fact," never a contrast word.

whyCorrect: The goal is to describe the process, so the right choice has to lay out the steps in order. Two notes supply them: an image is carved onto a printing block, and the block is then painted and stamped onto a print surface. Choice B is the only option that reports both steps in sequence.

whyWrong.A: This states that Lewis used relief printing but never says what relief printing involves, so no process is described.
whyWrong.C: This names lino cutting and mentions carving onto linoleum tile, but it stops before the painting and stamping steps and is about Lewis's particular work rather than the general process.
whyWrong.D: This lists possible block materials, which is a fact about relief printing, not a description of how it is carried out.

commonMistakes: Picking a choice that mentions the artist because she appears in the notes; the stated goal, not the notes' most prominent subject, decides what belongs in the sentence.

whyCorrect: The stem asks you to emphasize a similarity between two birds, so scan the notes for a trait both species share. The green-throated mango has a "long, black, curved bill" and the horned sungem has a "short, black, straight bill" — the shared element is that both bills are black. Choice C is the only option that puts the two birds side by side on a point they have in common.

whyWrong.A: This describes the guidebook and mentions no bird at all, so no similarity is drawn.
whyWrong.B: This puts the size difference in the main clause, so the emphasis lands on how the birds differ rather than on what they share.
whyWrong.D: This describes only the horned sungem, leaving nothing to compare it with.

tips: When two descriptions differ in most respects, read them attribute by attribute — here "black" is the single word that appears in both bill descriptions.

whyCorrect: The goal is to compare the two rivers' curviness, so the sentence must put one river above the other on that measure. The notes say the Embarras has high sinuosity and the Luni has low sinuosity, and that sinuosity is the ratio of stream length to valley length. Choice B states that the Embarras's ratio is greater than the Luni's, which is both accurate and an actual comparison.

whyWrong.A: This swaps the two rivers, calling the Luni high-sinuosity and the Embarras low-sinuosity, which contradicts the notes.
whyWrong.C: This says curviness is measured the same way for both rivers, which compares the method rather than the rivers.
whyWrong.D: This explains how sinuosity is calculated and never says which river is curvier.

commonMistakes: Checking only that a choice mentions both rivers; a comparison also has to assign them different positions on the trait in question.

whyCorrect: The colon means the rest of the sentence defines the blank, and what follows is a list of ways the program outperformed the old method: more accurate sidewalk identification, plus the ability to tell cobblestone from brick. The first sentence has already set up the road-map approach as "not very accurate." So the blank has to register the program as better, and "superior" is that word.

whyWrong.B: "Supportive" would mean the program reinforced the road-map method, but the passage sets the two up as rivals and reports the program beating one.
whyWrong.C: "Similar" flattens the comparison, and the evidence after the colon is entirely about differences in performance.
whyWrong.D: "Changed" states that the performance differed without saying in which direction, and it does not idiomatically take "to" in this construction.

tips: Read past the colon before choosing; the evidence there tells you not just that a comparison is being made but which way it runs.

whyCorrect: The frame "as ___ one another as storytelling and quilting" needs a phrase that describes a relationship between two art forms, and the surrounding sentences point to variety — "a wide variety of forms" before the blank and "these diverse arts" after it. Storytelling and quilting are cited as an extreme pair, so the blank must mean unlike. "Different from" is the only choice that fits both the meaning and the "as ... as" comparison.

whyWrong.A: "Confused with" would claim people mistake storytelling for quilting, which nothing in the passage suggests and which would undercut the point about variety.
whyWrong.B: "Humble about" describes an attitude a person holds, and art forms cannot be humble about each other.
whyWrong.C: "Useful to" would say the two forms serve each other, but the sentence is establishing range, not mutual benefit.

tips: The words "variety" and "diverse" bracket this blank on both sides; let them set the meaning before you test any choice.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says Miami theaters prefer pleasing audiences to taking risks. The second sets up a contrast with "while": eager to stage a known classic, but something else toward an unknown playwright's work. Since staging an unknown writer is the risky option, the blank must express reluctance, and "hesitant" is the direct opposite of the "eager" it is paired against.

whyWrong.A: "Surprised" describes a reaction to an unexpected event, not a theater's willingness to take on a production.
whyWrong.B: "Determined" means resolved to do it, which matches "eager" instead of contrasting with it and reverses the passage's logic about risk aversion.
whyWrong.C: "Fortunate" evaluates luck rather than willingness, and it would suggest theaters welcome the unknown playwright.

commonMistakes: Missing that "while ... might be eager" sets up an explicit contrast, so the blank must be roughly the opposite of "eager."

whyCorrect: The end of the sentence tells you the outcome: the sediments eventually form "new portions of land." For land to be built, material has to pile up at the point where the river meets the Gulf. "Accumulate" names that piling up and is the only choice consistent with new land appearing.

whyWrong.B: "Dissolve" means to break down into a liquid, which would remove the sediment rather than build anything from it.
whyWrong.C: "Accelerate" describes an increase in speed; sediment moving faster does not create landforms.
whyWrong.D: "Thrive" applies to living things that flourish, and sediment is not alive.

tips: When the sentence names a result, work backward from it — new land requires deposited material, so the verb has to be one of gathering.

whyCorrect: The sentence contrasts two research approaches with "Though," and it calls the second one "the novel path." Novel means new, so the studies described in the first half must be the established, usual ones. "Conventional" is the word for the standard approach that a novel path departs from.

whyWrong.A: "Eccentric" means unusual, which would put the earlier studies on the same side as the novel approach and destroy the contrast.
whyWrong.B: "Meager" means scanty, but the sentence says there are "many" such studies, so it contradicts the word right before the blank.
whyWrong.D: "Random" describes an absence of pattern, yet these studies share a consistent focus on people living above sea level.

tips: Find the word signaling the contrast — here "novel" — and make the blank its opposite.
